study.title: John 11 The Resurrection of Lazarus and the Way to Jesus" Death
study.overview: John 11 narrates the disease, death, and resurrection of Lazarus, showing that Jesus reacts not only as a healer, but as he who has authority over death and who reveals the glory of God at the time of suffering. The chapter also exposes the imperfect but growing faith of Martha and Mary, the real compassion of Jesus, the division caused by its signs and the political and religious reaction that accelerates the conspiracy against him. The narrative leads from Lazarus' to the plan to kill Jesus, making it clear that the miracle is at the same time a sign of life and announcement of the cross.

outline.title: Lazarus' disease, the delay of Jesus and the call to Judea
outline.explanation: Lazarus gets sick in Bethany, and his sisters send news to Jesus. He declares that sickness will serve the glory of God and remains two days where he is. He then decides to return to Judea, despite the risk of death, and teaches the disciples about walking in the light. The metaphor of sleep and death prepares the reader to understand that Jesus is not limited by the grave.

outline.title: The encounter with Martha and Mary: faith, lamentation and compassion of Jesus
outline.explanation: When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been dead for four days. Martha expresses repentance by the absence of Jesus, but also a limited trust in his power. Jesus presents himself as the resurrection and the life, asking for faith in this reality. Then, upon seeing Mary and those who weep, Jesus moves and weeps, revealing true sensitivity to death and human pain.

outline.title: The order at the tomb and the resurrection of Lazarus
outline.explanation: Faced with the stone of the tomb, Martha underscores the bad smell, but Jesus insists that faith will see the glory of God. He prays to the Father in public so that the crowd believes that he was sent by God, and then calls Lazarus out. The dead leave the tomb still encased in bands, and Jesus commands them to desate him, showing that his power overcomes death, but also that others should participate in the care and freedom of the risen.

outline.title: The division caused by the signal and the final conspiracy
outline.explanation: Many Jews believe to see the miracle, but others denounce Jesus to the Pharisees. The religious council fears losing position and provoke Roman reaction. Caiaphas prophesies, without fully realizing, that it is appropriate for a man to die for the people. From there, the decision to kill Jesus is established, he withdraws more in a more reserved way, and tension grows in Jerusalem as the Passover approaches. The chapter ends with an official order for anyone to know where Jesus is reporting it.

study.context: The chapter is located around Bethany, a village near Jerusalem, and mentions the approach of the Passover, when many went up to the city to purify themselves. The notes provided highlight that Bethany was near Jerusalem and that there was a great movement of pilgrims, which helped spread conversations about Jesus. The text also shows that the episode was remembered as a widely known public signal with a strong impact between religious leaders and the population.
study.theology: John 11 presents Jesus as Lord over death, not just as one who comforts in suffering. The statement I am the resurrection and life concentrates Christian hope on your own person, not just in a future event. The chapter unites power and compassion: Jesus knows what he will do, but we also truly weeps before the loss. This shows that biblical faith does not treat pain as an illusion; rather, it states that the glory of God can be revealed through it. At the same time, Lazarus' sign anticipates the very death and resurrection of Jesus, because the miracle provokes both faith and opposition. The speech of Caiaphas functions as involuntary prophecy: the death of Jesus will not be a political accident, but part of God's purpose to gather the scattered children of God. Thus, the chapter connects life, faith, cross, and unity of the people of God.

scholarViews.insight: The resurrection of Lazarus anticipates the very death and resurrection of Jesus; the tomb of Lazarus foreshadows the tomb of Jesus, and the sign already points to the hour of his glorification.
Jesus manifests true tenderness in suffering from the bereaved friends; his tears show the depth of his compassion before death and human pain.
Jesus raises his eyes to the Father and prays publicly so that the crowd knows that the miracle proceeds from the power of God, not from any other source.

questions: How would Jesus" statement that sickness would serve for the glory of God confronts our expectations of suffering and divine response time?
What does it mean, in practice, to believe in Jesus as the resurrection and life when we still face real grief, fear and loss?
How did the sign that brought faith in some also revealed the resistance of others, and what does it teach about the human response to the gospel?
study.practice: Read this chapter as an invitation to trust in Christ before you see the solution. When the wait seems long, remember that Jesus did not lose control when it takes time; when the pain is intense, remember that he weeps with those who weep; when faith seems small, hold on to what he said about himself. A concrete practice is to bring to God, in prayer, a situation that seems "dead" in his life to faith, relationship, encouragement or hope - and to ask him to reveal his glory, submitting himself to his way and time.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow us to determine with certainty all the historical details beyond what the chapter itself states and what the commentators mention in general. Some observations of Tyndale and Adam Clarke depend on textual reconstructions or comparisons that are not verifiable only to the biblical text provided; therefore they were used only as interpretations, not as uncontroversial facts. It is also not possible to confirm, from these notes, all the precise circumstances of the writing of the gospel or the chronology of each event.
